title: Everything that breathes (Psalm 150)
hookLine: the book ends: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD"
carry: let every thing that hath breath praise the Lord

lines: THE LAST SONG OF THE CONCERT.
cards: A great concert doesn't end quietly. The band brings everything in at once: drums, horns, guitars, the crowd singing along, the lights all on. On the last song, nobody holds anything back.
The Book of Psalms ends the same way. After a hundred and forty-nine songs of joy and grief, fear and hope, exile and homecoming, the very last psalm is pure, loud, everything-at-once praise.
And its final line is about something you're doing right now. Breathing.

teach.b: Psalm one fifty is short, only six verses, and almost every line starts the same way: hallelu, praise. Praise God in His sanctuary. Praise Him for His mighty acts.
Then the instruments pour in: the blast of the shofar, harp and lyre, drum and dance, strings and pipe, loud cymbals, crashing cymbals. It's the whole orchestra of ancient Israel, all at once.
Then the last line of the whole book: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." Hallelujah. After all the instruments, the final one is breath.
Not only priests or Levites or musicians: every person, every animal, anyone who can draw air.
Jews say this psalm every morning, near the end of the psalms of praise that open the service, and many repeat that last line twice, to mark the end.

The rabbis noticed that the word for breath, neshamah, is also the word for soul. A midrash plays on it: read neshamah as neshimah, a single breath, and it says, for every single breath you take, praise God.
Not once a day. Every breath. So the Book of Psalms, and these two weeks of psalms, end with breath.
They began with a tree by the water, then the stars, the shepherd, the mountain, the open hand, a song for each day, Hallel, and Shabbat.
This week: the rivers of Babylon, the depths, the mountains, Elul, sowing in tears, refuah shlemah, and now, everything that breathes.

how: Psalm 150 is said every morning as the last of the psalms of praise (Pesukei de-Zimra), and many repeat its final verse to mark the end of the Book of Psalms.

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.

s: the Book of Psalms ends quietly
it ends with trumpets, harps, drums, cymbals, and every breath.
Psalm 150 is said every morning in the Jewish service
as the last of the psalms of praise, often with its final line said twice.
a midrash reads the last line as: praise God for every single breath
neshamah, soul, heard as neshimah, a breath.

games.q: the Book of Psalms has named shofar, harp, lyre, drum, pipe and cymbals. what's the final instrument?
games.why: let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD. after the whole orchestra, the last instrument is breath.

practice: Close your eyes if you like, and take one slow breath in and one slow breath out: that breath is the last instrument of the Book of Psalms.
Keep breathing, and with each breath out let one small thanks go with it, for the air, for your body, for someone you love, for this day; you don't need words, the breath can carry it.
If you pray, say the last line: let every thing that hath breath praise the Lord.

wordCard.voice: Neshamah. Breath, and soul — the last line of the Book of Psalms calls on everything that has it to praise the Lord, every single breath.

orig.note: Hebrew: let everything that breathes praise Yah, the last line of Psalms.

carryVoice: Your line: let every thing that hath breath praise the Lord. The last instrument is the one you're already playing. And that's the whole Book of Psalms.

sources.q: Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD.
